title: Commerce adds Megaspeed and six affiliates to Entity List over AI-chip diversion risk
subtitle: The final rule covers entities across Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand — including an Alibaba cloud unit — with license applications now facing a presumption of denial.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security on November 23 added Megaspeed International Pte and six affiliated companies to the Entity List in a final rule. The listing cites the risk that the companies could divert advanced computing items to unauthorized end users or end uses. The seven entities span Singapore (Megaspeed International, Apex Enterprise Solutions, Swiftdata), Malaysia (MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International, Speedmatrix), and Thailand (Megaspeed Thailand). All items subject to the Export Administration Regulations now require a license, with applications reviewed under a presumption of denial.

The core allegation is chip transshipment to China. US authorities have investigated Megaspeed — a Nvidia cloud partner — since 2024 over whether it has been rerouting advanced AI accelerators to Chinese customers. Alibaba's Singapore unit Apex Enterprise Solutions was caught in the net; Alibaba called the listing a mistake and said it plans to fight it. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said other agencies had backed the listing 'for months' but that 'Commerce holds the pen.'

This is the second major enforcement action in a week, after the House committee disclosure on November 22 that a US revenue-share arrangement attached to roughly 580,000 Nvidia chips worth of China revenue. Together they signal that the enforcement delta — between what export controls say on paper and what actually happens in practice — is closing. For hyperscalers and GPU buyers in the three named countries, the practical effect is immediate: no more legal purchases of advanced US chips without an unlikely license.

A note for learners: export controls on AI chips are now functionally a global supply-chain problem, not just a US-China one. When you read that a company has a footprint in Singapore, Malaysia, or Thailand, that is now a regulatory data point about chip access, not just a logistics choice. If you build infrastructure that depends on a specific GPU, read the Entity List updates the way you'd read a tariff schedule — the rules can change your bill of materials overnight.
